title: Can both threads read 0?
sub: x = y = 0. Thread 1: x = 1; r1 = y. Thread 2: y = 1; r2 = x.

frames.caption: The store-buffering test. Thread 1 runs x = 1 then r1 = y; thread 2 runs y = 1 then r2 = x; x and y start at 0. Under sequential consistency, the result must match some interleaving of the two programs in which each thread's order is kept.
Each row is one such interleaving, and the result it produces.
All 6 interleavings. r1 = r2 = 0 never appears: whichever load runs last, the other thread's store has already happened. Under sequential consistency, at least one thread must see a 1.
Real CPUs, including x86, put each store into a per-core store buffer and keep going, rather than waiting for it to reach memory.
Thread 1 executes x = 1. The store goes into core 1's buffer. Memory still says x = 0.
Thread 2 executes y = 1. Same thing: buffered in core 2, invisible to core 1.
Thread 1 loads y. Its own buffer has nothing for y, so it reads memory: r1 = 0. Thread 2 loads x the same way: r2 = 0.

Only now do the buffers drain to memory. Both stores happened, yet both loads saw 0: an outcome no interleaving can produce. This is exactly the one reordering x86's TSO allows (a load passing an earlier store to a different address). The fix is an mfence between the store and the load, or making the operations seq_cst atomics, which inserts it for you.
